statement: In mathematics, a function from a set X to a set Y assigns to each element of X exactly one element of Y, denoted f: X -> Y. The set X is called the domain of the function and the set Y is called the codomain of the function.

symbols.meaning: function from set X to set Y
an element of the domain X
the unique element of Y assigned to x by f (image of x under f)

properties.property: Given a function f: X -> Y, its graph is formally the set G = {(x, f(x)) | x in X}
properties.why: formal set-theoretic specification pairing each domain element with its uniquely assigned codomain value

properties.property: The image f(x) of any element x in X is always a single element of Y, but the preimage f^{-1}(y) = {x in X | f(x) = y} of an element y in Y may be empty or contain any number of elements
properties.why: the uniqueness condition applies directedly from the domain to the codomain

properties.property: The composition g ∘ f: X -> Z of functions f: X -> Y and g: Y -> Z is defined by (g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)); it is associative ((h ∘ g) ∘ f = h ∘ (g ∘ f)) but generally not commutative
properties.why: composition is an operation chaining sequential evaluation where codomain of the first equals the domain of the second

properties.property: The identity functions id_X and id_Y satisfy f ∘ id_X = id_Y ∘ f = f
properties.why: identity mappings leave elements unchanged under composition

properties.property: A function f: X -> Y is bijective if and only if it is both injective (f(a) != f(b) for all a != b) and surjective (f(X) = Y), which holds if and only if it admits an inverse function g: Y -> X such that g ∘ f = id_X and f ∘ g = id_Y
properties.why: bijectivity ensures that every y in Y has exactly one preimage in X

assumptions.assumption: Each element x in the domain X must be mapped to exactly one element y in the codomain Y
assumptions.breaks_when: An element of X has no assignment in Y, or is assigned multiple distinct elements in Y

assumptions.assumption: Function composition g ∘ f is defined only if the codomain of f matches the domain of g
assumptions.breaks_when: The codomain of f is not equal to the domain of g

failure_modes.signature: A relation associates an input x with more than one output value in Y
failure_modes.cause: Failing to select a single value for each element of the domain when working with relations such as x^2 + y^2 = 1 without specifying a branch
The codomain of f does not equal the domain of g

failure_modes.signature: No function g: Y -> X satisfies both g ∘ f = id_X and f ∘ g = id_Y
failure_modes.cause: f fails to be injective (multiple inputs map to the same output) or fails to be surjective (some codomain elements have empty preimage)
